newsitem.title: POLAND: SPEED SKATING-GOLDEN TREBLE FOR NIEMANN.
newsitem.headline: SPEED SKATING-GOLDEN TREBLE FOR NIEMANN.

text.p: Germany's Gunda Niemann cruised to her third gold medal in three days at the world speed skating single distance championships on Sunday as Dutch and German skaters continued to dominate.

Niemann, who earlier won gold over 3,000 and 5,000 metres, completed the women's 1,500 metre competition in 2 minutes 4.43 seconds, nearly two seconds faster than silver medallist Anni Friesinger, also of Germany.
Marianne Timmer of the Netherlands was third, more than three seconds behind Niemann, who now has an unprecedented nine world titles to her name.
"I was tired after the 3,000 and 5,000 metre races and I am happy I had enough strength to win this one," Niemann said.
Niemann, 30, added she expected the 1998 Winter Olympics in Nagano, Japan, to be her last important competition.
"The next Olympics will likely be my last big event."

During the three-day single distance world championships Dutch and German skaters won 23 out of a possible 30 medals, with Norway's Adne Sondral breaking the two-country shut-out on Sunday with a gold in the men's 1,000 metre race.
Sondral won in 1:14.40 ahead of Jan Bos and Martin Hersman of the Netherlands to get his first world championship.
"I finally won a world championship and the key was a very tight last lap," Sondral said, adding he was happy to break the spell Dutch and German skaters have had over their competitors.
"There are many high quality Dutch and German skaters and even if one of them does badly others can fill in the gap, so its fun to beat them," Sondray said.
Dutchman Gianni Romme won the men's 10,000 metre race in 14:18.75, nearly 12 seconds ahead of compatriot Rintje Ritsma and 15 ahead of Bob de Jong, also from the Netherlands.
The race was sweet revenge for Romme, who lost a close 5,000 metres race to Ritsma two days earlier.
"I was a little tired after two days of competition but Romme was just too strong in the 10 km," said Ritsma, also winner of the 1,500 metres race on Saturday.
The head of the International Skating Union (ISU) Ottavio Cinquanta said the next world championships would again be held on an outdoor oval despite criticism from skaters.
"There will be other championships held in the open air...this is the way the sport started more than 100 years ago," Cinquanta told a news briefing after the event.
Skaters had voiced concern over holding such an important event outdoors, as in Warsaw, because variable winds made skating difficult.
